hints: Look closely at the centre of the cell in Fig. 6.1 for the darkest stained structures - what molecule becomes highly condensed and visible during mitosis?
walkthrough:
Spot Where DNA Lives During Mitosis**
DNA is packaged with histone proteins to form chromosomes. During mitosis the chromosomes condense tightly, so they stain very dark and become easy to see under the microscope.

Point to the Right Structure**
In Fig. 6.1 the dark V-shaped bodies in the middle are the separating chromosomes, each made of a chromatid containing DNA. A clear line labelled D to any one of those dark bodies earns the mark.
Final answer: Line labelled D pointing to any dark-stained chromatid / chromosome in the centre of the cell.

hints: Focus on the dark chromosomes - are they lined up as one row in the middle, or have they split into two groups moving apart toward opposite ends?
walkthrough:
Read the Chromosome Position**
In prophase chromosomes are scattered and condensing. In metaphase sister chromatids line up in a single row at the equator. Here you can see two distinct dark groups with a clear gap in the middle, moving away from each other.

Link Movement to Anaphase**
Separation of sister chromatids at the centromere and movement toward opposite poles pulled by the spindle is the defining event of anaphase. That is exactly what Fig. 6.1 shows.

hints: Start by recalling what microtubules normally build in prophase and what that structure looks like in the micrograph - look for the faint radiating lines spreading out from the poles.
Now link structure to function - if that microtubule structure was working normally, what would it have done to the chromosomes by anaphase, and can you see that result in Fig. 6.1?
walkthrough:
Remember What Colchicine Blocks**
Spindle fibres are made of microtubules that are organised in prophase. The spindle attaches to chromosomes at the centromere and pulls sister chromatids apart in anaphase. Colchicine stops microtubule organisation, so no functional spindle would form.

Use the Visible Spindle as Evidence**
In Fig. 6.1 you can clearly see the spindle with radiating spindle fibres running from pole to chromosome. If colchicine had acted, this organised spindle would be absent or disrupted.

Use Chromatid Separation as Evidence**
The sister chromatids have already separated into two groups and are moving to opposite poles. That movement only happens when spindle fibres shorten by disassembly of microtubules. This proves the cell completed prophase and metaphase normally and entered anaphase, so it was not treated with colchicine.

Final answer: Fully formed spindle / spindle fibres visible; sister chromatids attached to spindle microtubules and have separated and moved toward opposite poles, showing spindle functioned normally.
